title: Fallacy exposed: a sufficient faith-rule need not prove itself — like science's first principles
source_text: XXXI. Ut vero sophistici istius argumenti fallacia detegatur, notandum est illud tanquam rem manifestam supponere id quod falsissimum est, nempe, non esse illam sufficientem fidei regulam cujus testimonio non possint omnia probari quae ad fidem pertinent, ne quidem excepta illa ipsa regula. Nam, quaecunque tandem fidei regula statuatur, non potest illa proprio testimonio probari. Nihil enim seipsum hoc modo probare potest, cum probatio omnis sit ex notioribus, idem vero seipso non sit notius, & ignotius. Et tamen res est maxime ad fidem pertinens, & necessaria, ut ipsam fidei regulam amplectamur, & illi certum assensum praebeamus. Igitur illa fidei regula perfecta est & sufficiens, non quae seipsam probat, sed ex qua supposita probari possunt omnia, praeter ipsam, quae ad fidem pertinent. Ideoque quamvis Scriptura proprio testimonio sufficienter probari non possit, hoc tamen non arguit illam non esse perfectam & sufficientem fidei regulam. Et dicere Scripturam non sufficere ad probanda omnia quae fidei sunt, quoniam proprio suo testimonio fidem sibi facere non potest, sophisticari est eodem plane modo ac si quis probaret coelum non omnia tegere quoniam coelum non tegit ipsum caelum: aut cujusdam scientiae principia non esse veluti normam & regulam, per quam probantur omnia quae ad illam scientiam spectant: quoniam ipsa principia per principia non probantur; Et tamen ad aliquam scientiam pertinet illius principia nosse.
pass_a_gloss: But that the fallacy of that sophistic argument may be uncovered, it is to be noted that it takes as manifest what is most false, namely, that that is not a sufficient rule of faith by whose testimony all things which pertain to faith cannot be proved, not even excepting that rule itself. For, whatever rule of faith is finally established, it cannot be proved by its own testimony. For nothing can prove itself in this way, since every proof is from things better known, and the same thing is not better known than itself, and less known. And yet it is a matter most pertaining to faith, and necessary, that we embrace the rule of faith itself, and give it certain assent. Therefore that rule of faith is perfect and sufficient which does not prove itself, but from which, being supposed, all things can be proved, besides itself, which pertain to faith. And therefore although Scripture cannot be sufficiently proved by its own testimony, this nevertheless does not argue that it is not a perfect and sufficient rule of faith. And to say that Scripture does not suffice for proving all things which are of faith, because by its own testimony it cannot make faith for itself, is to sophisticate in exactly the same way as if someone proved that the sky does not cover all things because the sky does not cover the sky itself: or that the principles of some science are not as it were a norm and rule by which all things which belong to that science are proved: because the principles themselves are not proved by principles; And yet it belongs to some science to know its principles.
pass_b_english: The sophistic fallacy assumes what is false: that a sufficient faith-rule must prove everything including itself.
No rule of faith can prove itself by its own testimony — proof is from what is better known, and a thing is not better known than itself.
Yet embracing the rule is itself necessary to faith.
A perfect sufficient rule is one that, once supposed, proves all else of faith — not one that proves itself.
Scripture's inability to prove itself by bare self-testimony does not strip its sufficiency.
Saying otherwise is like saying the sky does not cover all because it does not cover itself — or that science's first principles are no rule because principles do not prove principles.
